items.detaildHeader: A Punjabi Palimpsest: Cultural Memory and Amnesia at the Aam Khas Bhag
items.description:
This project explores the dynamics of applying participant observation, anthropological filmmaking, oral history and interactive design to tackle issues of 'cultural amnesia' in a town of post-partition Punjab. The project's aim was to forge new relationships with a contested past in order to protect Mughal heritage sites that become targets of vandalism as a result of past politico-religious tensions. Concentrating on Sirhind, a province in Punjab, located on the historical Grand Trunk Road.

Working as an ethnographer and interaction designer in the 3 member team to develop immersive narrations of oral histories. An initial period of research and a subsequent stage of skill sharing, students of local colleges researched the heritage of their town as cultural palimpsest and presented their work in one of town's oldest Mughal monuments, 'Aam Khas Bagh', a 17th century royal Mughal Sarai. The public event was attended by 400 people.

Project funding was by the Arts & Humanities Research Council, United Kingdom. It was an assignment based undertaking for the project 'A Punjabi Palimpsest: Cultural Memory and Amnesia at the Aam Khas Bhag'. The endeavour was undertaken under the guidance of University of Surrey and British Council. This was in partnership with Cultural Resource Conservation Initiative, to build ground up community based heritage conservation systems. The intention of the project being to nominate the 'Grand Trunk Road' as a UNESCO world heritage site.

items.detaildHeader: Appetite: A board game on food, with food
items.description:
Food, today, is inextricably caught up in a web of politics, controversy, and host of issues, the emergence of which can be traced back to the industry, media and corporation led practices of production and distribution, fortified by mindless consumption in the urban setting.

Looking at the overall landscape of this issue, an experimental intervention was devised taking the form of participatory game-based installation. It was conceived as part of the residency program InContext:public.art.ecology at Khoj International Artists Association, New Delhi. The objective was to initiate a public dialogue around food issues through art and design interventions.

The allegorical play offers an insight into the mindless culture of consumption, in context to contemporary food and purchasing practices. The game mechanics in it itself carries the message. In a limited number of turns and moves that the player must negotiate, the game play attempts to explain the journey as a consumer confronted with the paradox of choice in everyday life. The tendency of people to blindly follow rules in a game is metaphorical to the real life scenario, that we find ourselves embroiled in. Intentional missing explanations induce complicity and some hard hitting truths are unearthed towards the end, inducing staggering reactions.

items.description:
‘We are what we eat’- This is an epigram which validates our long-standing relationship with food. Food besides being a subject of endless passionate discussion within our personal and most intimate lives has historically been a significant indicator of our cultural, ecological and social realms.

‘Story of Urban Food Chain’ – a public art experiment’ represents the vitality of food design and explores food concepts beyond the table through a technology driven installation with food items as interfaces. So food items acts as a medium to interact, explore, engage in reiterating consumer choices in everyday life.

The installation is a social experiment to gauge individual reactions to the narrative as well as to the aural and visual interfaces, focussing on the subtle indications towards participants’ food choices. The audience acts as the consumer where he/she goes through the different aspects of the food chain that is part of their daily lives and sees the the paradox of choice.

To bring out the paradox, the installation, is constructed on the intersection of new media and food, where food and technology traverse at a common meeting ground resulting in varied results. Through carefully crafted interactions and an element of humour in the dialogues, people can interpret the story of the ‘Urban Food Chain’. It uses ubiquitous objects and interactions of everyday life, with an objective to subconsciously alter the perceptions of individuals; to be able to encourage them to question the existing urban food culture and make informed decisions as a consumer.

The installation offers an insight into our urban food chain, where everything is controlled by corporations, branding and politics driven by the capitalist mindsets. Consumers are left devoid of choices, burdened with unanswered questions, health issues and inflation.

items.detaildHeader: Entrée: Reflecting on the Future of a Meal
items.description:
Entree is a project that, through the lens of experimental media, intends to launch an investigation into what the technologically riddled future of a meal could entail, be it the far future, or the very next month.

Food can be regarded as a medium that constantly connects time, space and memories of a world that one grew up in to that in which one will grow old. In a manner that is both tangible and intangible, it links the present to the past and transcends into the future.

Post the era of industrialization, the production, distribution, and consumption of food are and always have been troubled with complex issues ranging from industrialization to globalization. Wherein the food we eat and closely associate ourselves with, is marked by its own journey through the road of cultural, industrial, and ecological changes. With traces of chemical elements, toxic materials, and other unknowns in consumables, it is the meal in this post-media age that has been put under the scanner in this project.

The hyper-mediated experience addresses the painful truth of reality by embracing the blissful ignorance of illusion, created by the presence of choice. In a world inundated with choice, the mechanical and automated nature of the meal embodies the paradox of choicelessness, given the prison of consumption which our bodies are born into. The space, in its unfeeling morbidness seeks to recreate an imagery, of this very prison, a warped reflection of our lives, that one can realize or simply overlook.The desire to exit and return to the reality is invoked, but not without leaving one questioning about the real and the surreal, fact and fiction, with respect to what we commonly perceive as 'food' and nourishment.

items.description:
Objects like tables are different from any other multimodal artefacts given the importance of their practical function. Tables are multimodal and semiotic artefacts.

A round table (referred, IKEA study of tables) surface is constructed in two layers, the top is a non conductive layer and the bottom is a conductive layer formed by a metal sheet. They together would act as a capacitance sensing device. With the help of customized electronics and code, the table detects the number of fingers placed and the pressure applied on the surface of the table. Each touch interaction is relayed as readings from the micro-controller. Visuals were put into place to interpret the readings in a simpler fashion. The table top is used for projection of content.

The activities that we perform daily around the dining table like sitting, picking up a spoon, eating, sharing etc. were intended as interactions which can have a mediated output. The content for the output can be mapped and projected on to the surface of the table while food is consumed.

The table is an important cultural artefact in the act “to eat”. In the idealistic situation the table can act as a self sustaining aquaponic structure. It will support plant and aquatic life which can become part of the food chain of the person. Herbs, vegetables can be grown alongside with fishes. They help in providing each other with the needed nutrients and oxygen to survive. The surface of the table will offer immediate value and the plants/ fishes will suggest contemplation value. The table’s intent is to motivate people to live a sustainable locavore lifestyle.

‘Physis’ is a Greek word which translates to english as ‘Nature.’ It is the principle of growth or change in nature.

Rapid fusions of computing and dwelling spaces, as well as the increasingly tactile and gestural nature of interactions with digital devices act as motivation for the following explorations. If a broad variety of objects in living, social and working spaces are made aware and responsive to human presence, touch and gesture; what will be the outcome?

In the series of experimentation with living plants, ubiquitous technology is used. Plants were transformed as highly expressive and interactive user interfaces (referred, Botanicus Interactus). The prototypes use customized electronics and computing with living flora. The outcome is an interaction platform that takes interactions from the physical to a digital environment.

The technology used has a number of unique properties. This instrumentation of plants is simple, non-invasive, and does not damage the plants. It requires only a single wire placed anywhere in the soil. The interaction with plant goes beyond simple touch and allows rich gestural interaction. Examples include sliding fingers on the stem or leaf, detecting touch and grasp location, tracking proximity, and estimating the amount of pressure on touch.

A broad range of applications are possible with the developed technology, designing interactive responsive environments and new forms of living interaction devices as well as developing organic ambient and pervasive interfaces.

It is for children from the age group of 3 to 5 years. At this age the kids start to learn about colors, numbers, different fruits and vegetables. It is based on the practice of play, which is important for learning at this young age. It is also influenced by the Psychology of Flow which is an important phase of learning and doing.

The prototype is made in the form of a planter, with different fruits and vegetables. The fruits and vegetables are in the form of stuffed plant signs. Plant signs are put in planters to indicate the seed that has been sowed in the pot. These interactive plant signs come to life when planted in the planter. Individual fruit or vegetable is imparted with a specific character. These are then transformed into a narrative structure with dialogues.

The interaction indicates the act of planting and gratification. When a tomato is planted the tomato will talk back to the child with information. The related content will be kind of plants, the colour of fruit, classification and some fun facts. When a second plant is planted into the planter a short dialogue happens between the two plants. The conversation will be from daily life; for example how the two are related or used in everyday food.

The intent of the concept is to introduce children to the idea of planting. Giving them knowledge about our day-to-day food arriving from plants, how they are grown and where they come from. The children can be taught the idea of “growing your own food”. So that when they grow up they can live a more sustainable lifestyle.

It is an exploration with food and sound. Distinct tunes are played according to the kind of eatables in your plate. The production of music takes place through a smart handheld device. The handheld gadget is made out of customized electronics and acts as a food scanner. It has the ability to scan your food and generate musical notes accordingly.

The food on your plate acts as an input to produce music. Generated music from food is based on the thought; if food had the ability to talk to you, what would it say? Would it sing? Maybe it would sing or speak in a gentle murmuring tone; crooning its way to your stomach and heart.

Eating is multisensory in nature and the device enhances the sensorial hearing aspect of your food, through producing sounds. It enhances the experience around food and of eating. Every sound clip produced will be specific to the nature of the food on your plate. Particular food items will have specific sounds; it will depend on the colour, the quality and the quantity. With further work it can have the ability to distinguish and detect fast food so that it can produce corresponding shocking sounds.

The device will also have the ability to send the produced sound clips to other people, using similar devices or over social media websites. So that other people can hear the kind of food you are eating. It can also have an effect on people’s consumption patterns, as they would relate certain sounds to be good and certain sound to be dire, consequential to the foods that produce it. It will give rise to a subconscious equation of good and bad foods.

The idea of reflection, enhances the capability of play. People like to play with their shadows and reflections, they want to see themselves perform. In reflection is a concept to signify ‘You are what you eat’, as mentioned in the Indian texts ‘Upanishads’.

It can be interpreted that food constitutes us, builds us and makes us, so we are formed by the kind of food we eat. By telling what you eat we can estimate who you are.

The reflection of the person is enclosed within a frame, but the reflection is not straightforward. Rather than a simple reflected surface the reflection is influenced by the kind of food that constitutes you (referred, artist Giuseppe Arcimboldo).

The conceptual prototype uses the abilities of a webcam to detect presence. It captures the silhouette and colours of the person’s image and translates it into a reflection into the picture frame. It is a generated image, composed of different foods, fruits and vegetables. Computational abilities will derive selection of the food items through different colours. For example colour red can be formed by tomatoes or cherries depending on the intensity and tone of red in the image. So the reflected silhouette of the person is composed of tomatoes, wheat etc.

The thought can also comment on the consumption patterns of people as the image formed can be through choice of food. It can denote the kind of consumer culture we live in through the medium of a self portrait.

Ethnography project to understand the Aural Life World of an Ethnic group to map lived experiences and aural landscapes. To make sense of sounds which may not exist in the real world but have meanings for the group or the community by making a visual artefact.

items.detaildHeader: Records for Life: Re-evaluation and Re-design of a Healthcard Framework
items.description:
Center for Knowledge Societies (CKS) along with the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF) and the World Health Organisation (WHO) provided a platform for bringing the worlds of health, research and design together. The project studied health systems around child immunisation. The scope of work, laid out in phases, revolved around understanding how a health card, figures in the health ecology of three countries, namely-Bihar, Kenya and Indonesia. Understand existing cultural influences on immunisation and how they can be taken care, in designing a digital format for health records.

As part of the project, we also managed a global crowdsourcing design challenge. Evaluation framework was created to select 30 cards from 433 entries of a crowdsourcing competition and testing them in these respective countries to compare and understand various aspects of the chosen cards that work with the target audience.

Qualitative and quantitative research methods were applied to collect data. This data provided insights which were then used to create high impact designs and suggest technological recommendations.

Field work was followed by post field analysis of the three locations resulting in various internal workshops, discussions and brainstorming sessions. The analysis was summed up as design recommendations in a Records for Life report and presentation given to a panel of experts from WHO, UNICEF, BMGF, IxDA, GAVI in London.

It was a proud and humbling moment when Melinda Gates named CKS as one of the nine players in the world changing the face of Routine Immunization and Records for Life was named as one of the projects doing just that.

For the entire article, please click: http://www.theguardian.com/global-development-professionals-network/2014/apr/28/melinda-gates-vaccines-immunisation-list?CMP=twt_gu

items.detaildHeader: Taj Ganj: Taking Our Heritage Forward
items.description:
Research project for developing an integrated heritage-based development plan for Taj Ganj, Agra for the Directorate of Tourism, Uttar Pradesh, India. Taj Ganj, the ‘Heritage Precinct’, as defined by UNESCO. It is the area right outside the forecourt of Taj Mahal, that houses the the descendants of the artisans who built Taj Mahal and is home to cultural and built heritage, age old crafts, traditions and practices.

As part of a team of field researchers from National Institute of Design, the brief was to study the irregular and unbalanced flow of tourist traffic through the 3 entry gates to the Taj: East, West and South, that happen to lie right in the periphery of Taj Ganj. The idea was to create systems to regularize tourist traffic and to make inclusive experiences without disrupting the socio-cultural fabric of the place. My area of study was the residential area leading to the West Gate, one of the gates that attracts heavy tourist traffic.The process followed was the classic phenomenological approach of ethnography which included engaging with the community, building a rapport, gaining access to the site and its gatekeepers, detailed observations and rigorous documentation. Long Interviews and Participant Observations were the fundamental instruments used in this research during the two week period. I conducted mapping exercises to also understand the different demographics of the people living in the area.

Finally, data from the team members were collated into a report. Thereafter a master plan for modernization and building sustainable livelihoods, conservation of built heritage, protecting intangible cultural heritage assets and unique visitor experiences is now in the process of development and implementation.

Working in the Social Science Research team within Next Experiences with Technology (NXT) Group. Undertaking research for Tizen's entry level smartphone for Indian market, to define India specific features that can be incorporated in the new OS & device.

Conducting user experience research for mobiles and wearables in the areas of healthcare and fitness.

Understanding social and psychological implications in human computer trust and computer mediated communication.

It is an ongoing research and development endeavour. My journey with food continues and my appetite keeps increasing. It is a continuation of my master’s thesis project where I explored food politics through self initiated research and artworks, making people aware of the convoluted food system that we live in. Travelling further on the road I started growing some of my own food, through organic urban farming. I ventured out into my own edible terrace garden which inspired me to again merge technology and the urban farming. This endeavour lead me to develop a prototype of a smart planter which can monitor growth of plants through a series of sensors and applications. I disembarked from the project as I learned the intricacies of organic farming and found the project to be trivial in nature when compared to the monetary or intrinsic value. After having seen the work of Open Agricultures Lab, I am now trying to build a frugal aeroponic structure with the help of a makerspace in Bangalore.

In my upcoming work I would want to look at disrupting urban living spaces and systems to reconfigure the urban life towards more ecological point of view which can define the future of not only food and living spaces but also break the paradox of choice. Making technology and food accessible to everyone.

Bangalore is the fourth most populous city in India. It has a high migration rate of its working population, mostly because of software industry. With people having high disposable income they are focused towards improving the quality of daily life. There is a huge amount of interest and inclination towards eating fresh, organic food.

But the present cost, convenience and availability are major factor influencing food trends, the current demand and supply chain is unbalanced.

Existing independent systems in this segment cater to their respective needs, we here propose to interconnect them through technology, to bring about an impactful change.
